metadata.working_title: Sixty-five year old man, worsening breathlessness, brought in by EMS
metadata.final_diagnosis: Acute decompensated heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (acute on chronic), presenting as hypertensive acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema, precipitated by loop diuretic non-adherence and dietary sodium load.
learning_objectives: Recognise the warm-and-wet (Nohria profile B) presentation of acute decompensated HFrEF, and state why distinguishing it from cold-and-wet changes the treatment.
Sequence non-invasive positive pressure ventilation and vasodilation ahead of diuresis in hypertensive acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema, and justify that ordering.

Identify interventions that are actively harmful in acute decompensated HFrEF: intravenous beta blockade, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockade, crystalloid bolus, and inotropes in a hypertensive well-perfused patient.

Interpret natriuretic peptide, high-sensitivity troponin, ECG, chest radiograph and POCUS as supportive rather than diagnostic, and distinguish non-ischaemic (type 2) troponin elevation from acute coronary occlusion.
Elicit the precipitant of decompensation on history, treating 'why did this patient decompensate now' as part of the resuscitation rather than an afterthought.
Anticipate post-intubation haemodynamic collapse in a preload-dependent vasodilated patient, and manage it without a fluid bolus.
metadata.teaching_frame: Nohria/Stevenson profile B (warm and wet). The case is deliberately the stereotypical presentation: the intent is pattern consolidation, not diagnostic difficulty.

care_setting.label: Quaternary care, Level 1 trauma centre
care_setting.detail: Adult emergency department. Full laboratory, imaging and blood bank on site. Cardiology, critical care, cardiothoracic surgery and interventional cardiology are available in house at all hours. Nothing in this case is limited by resources.
care_setting.provenance: Setting is a deployment property, not a clinical fact. It is authored per case so that a case written for a critical access hospital can say so, because the correct disposition depends on it.

arrival.line: Brought in by EMS. Handover given on arrival in the resuscitation bay.

patient.background: Ischaemic cardiomyopathy with HFrEF, LVEF 25-30% on echocardiogram eight months ago. Anterior STEMI six years ago treated with a drug-eluting stent to the left anterior descending artery. Hypertension. Type 2 diabetes mellitus. Chronic kidney disease stage 3 with a baseline creatinine of 1.4 mg/dL. Ex-smoker, 30 pack-years, stopped at the time of his infarct. Untreated obstructive sleep apnoea (declined CPAP two years ago). Home medications: furosemide 40 mg daily, carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, sacubitril/valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 81 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg twice daily.
patient.presenting_vitals_source: Inherited from phase 'presentation'. EMS applied a nasal cannula at 6 L/min en route and established no intravenous access.
patient.presenting_appearance: A heavy-set older man sitting bolt upright on the EMS stretcher, gripping the rails, visibly sweating and speaking in two or three word bursts. He will not lie flat and pushes the trolley back up when it is lowered.
patient.ems_handover_text: Sixty-five year old man, known heart failure, three or four days of worsening breathlessness, much worse since about four this morning. Family called when he could not get up the stairs. Sats were 84 percent on room air at the house, 87 on six litres now. Pressure has been running high the whole way in, last was 190 over 100. He has not had any of his own medications for the last few days. No chest pain that he will admit to. Nothing given en route apart from oxygen.
patient.arrival_handover: Sixty-five year old man, breathing trouble that's been getting worse over the last few days. Family called us this morning when he couldn't manage the stairs, and he's still only holding 87% on six litres by nasal cannula.

prerequisites.failure_message: He's already got a tube in and he's on the ventilator. The mask won't do anything now.

prompt.text: He's working really hard to breathe and his sat is sitting at 87 on six litres. Do you want to do something more for his breathing? I can get the CPAP mask on him.

escalation.text: He's still tripoding and pulling with his neck muscles, sat's still 87. I've got CPAP and BiPAP both at the bedside. Do you want either of them on him?

case_actions.debrief_note: Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation is the single highest-value early intervention in acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema. It recruits flooded alveoli, reduces the work of breathing, and by raising intrathoracic pressure it reduces both preload and left ventricular transmural pressure, which lowers afterload. Applying it early is what allows most of these patients to avoid an endotracheal tube. Be honest with learners about the evidence: earlier meta-analyses reported reductions in intubation and mortality, but the largest randomised trial, 3CPO, found no difference in seven-day mortality or intubation rate versus standard oxygen therapy. The strongest defensible claim is faster symptomatic and physiological improvement, with intubation avoidance supported by meta-analytic but not by the single largest trial. On the choice between modes, which is one button here because it is one decision: continuous and bilevel positive pressure are equivalent for the purposes of this case. Bilevel adds inspiratory support and is often preferred when the patient is hypercapnic and tiring, as this one is with a pCO2 of 54. 3CPO found no difference between the two modes in mortality or intubation rate, so either is defensible and the decision that mattered was to apply positive pressure at all. The historical concern that bilevel increased myocardial infarction has not been borne out.
references: Gray A, Goodacre S, Newby DE, Masson M, Sampson F, Nicholl J; 3CPO Trialists. Noninvasive ventilation in acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema. N Engl J Med. 2008;359(2):142-51. [PubMed record checked]

Masip J, Roque M, Sanchez B, et al. Noninvasive ventilation in acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema: systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA. 2005;294(24):3124-30. [citation seen in secondary sources; verify]

Because one catalog entry resolves to one case action, the second was unreachable: its tag, debrief note and references never rendered, and a scenario step naming it was silently discarded. vital_effects.note: Three points, held for as long as the mask is on. Alveolar recruitment and the reduction in work of breathing are the mechanism, and they persist rather than wearing off, which is why there is no duration here. The guard removes it at intubation: the mask comes off, and the ventilator phases author their own saturation. The size is an author's teaching choice, not a measured quantity, and no trial supports a specific number.

prompt.text: His pressure is 188 over 104. Do you want anything for the blood pressure while we're sorting out his breathing?

case_actions.halt_reason: You started a nitroglycerin infusion in a patient whose blood pressure was already dependent on vasopressor support after intubation; the additional preload and afterload reduction collapsed his coronary perfusion pressure and he arrested.
case_actions.debrief_note: Afterload reduction is the pharmacological priority in hypertensive acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema. This patient is not primarily short of diuresis in the first ten minutes; he is short of forward flow against a systolic pressure of 188 with a failing ventricle, and a large part of his pulmonary edema is redistribution rather than accumulated total body water. Nitrates reduce preload at lower doses and afterload at higher ones, and the trial evidence supports a vasodilator-forward rather than diuretic-forward strategy in this specific phenotype. Doses used for this indication are considerably higher than the anti-anginal doses residents are used to. The same drug becomes harmful the moment the patient is hypotensive, which is why the tag on this action is phase-dependent rather than fixed.
references: Cotter G, Metzkor E, Kaluski E, et al. Randomised trial of high-dose isosorbide dinitrate plus low-dose furosemide versus high-dose furosemide plus low-dose isosorbide dinitrate in severe pulmonary edema. Lancet. 1998;351(9100):389-93. [PubMed record checked]
Heidenreich PA, et al. 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure. Circulation. 2022;145(18):e895-e1032. [UNVERIFIED, confirm before release]

vital_effects.note: Five points for thirty seconds, then back to baseline. Redistribution of pulmonary blood volume is fast and, at a fixed rate with no titration modelled, transient. Repeating the drug repeats the same excursion rather than adding to it: the key is shared with the sublingual route, so the two cannot be stacked into an improvement neither would produce. Deliberately unsatisfying, and the point of the case is that the durable gain comes from the mask.

case_actions.halt_reason: You gave sublingual nitroglycerin to a patient whose blood pressure was already dependent on vasopressor support after intubation; further vasodilation dropped his coronary perfusion pressure and he arrested.
case_actions.debrief_note: A reasonable bridge while an infusion is being mixed, and repeated sublingual dosing is a legitimate strategy when a pump is not immediately available. It is not a substitute for a titratable infusion in a patient who is going to need sustained afterload reduction, because the effect is short-lived and cannot be dialled back if the pressure falls too far. Credit here is partial: the right idea, an incomplete execution.

vital_effects.note: Same excursion as the infusion, same key, so the two routes do not stack.

prerequisites.failure_message: There's no nitro running at the moment, so there's nothing for me to stop.

prompt.text: His pressure is 74 over 46 and the nitro is still running at the rate you set. Do you want me to do something about that?

case_actions.debrief_note: Stopping the vasodilator is the first move in post-intubation hypotension in a patient on a nitrate infusion, and it is free. It is easy to reach for a pressor while the drug driving the hypotension continues to run. Turning the infusion off does not act instantly, which is why it is done alongside, not instead of, haemodynamic support.

prompt.text: He's breathing easier on the mask now. He told the medics he's been out of his water pill for the best part of a week. Do you want to give him a diuretic?

case_actions.debrief_note: This patient genuinely is volume overloaded, not only redistributed: four kilograms above his stated dry weight, five days without his loop diuretic, peripheral edema and a raised venous pressure. He needs diuresis. The teaching point is sequencing, not omission. Positive pressure and vasodilation act within minutes on the process that is threatening him now; the diuretic acts on the total body sodium and water that accumulated over days. Dose matters: a patient already on a loop diuretic at home requires more than a naive dose, and the conventional approach is to give at least two to two and a half times the home oral dose intravenously. The DOSE trial found no significant difference in its co-primary endpoints between high and low dose or between bolus and infusion, with the high-dose strategy showing better symptom relief on secondary measures at the cost of transient rises in creatinine, so present dosing as a reasoned choice rather than a rule.
references: Felker GM, Lee KL, Bull DA, et al. Diuretic strategies in patients with acute decompensated heart failure. N Engl J Med. 2011;364(9):797-805. [PubMed record checked]
Cotter G, et al. Lancet. 1998;351(9100):389-93. [PubMed record checked]
case_actions.no_vital_effect_note: Deliberate. Furosemide moves this patient into the improving phase, which lowers his heart rate, blood pressure and respiratory rate, and it carries no vital_effect, so the saturation on the monitor does not move at all. A resident who gives the diuretic first and watches the number sees nothing happen. That is the lesson.

case_actions.debrief_note: Unglamorous and rate-limiting. Every intravenous drug in this case is gated behind it, which is the point: the resident who orders a nitroglycerin infusion before anyone has a line has ordered something that cannot happen yet.

case_actions.display_name: Continuous cardiac monitoring and pulse oximetry
case_actions.debrief_note: Standard for any patient with acute dyspnoea and known cardiomyopathy. In this case the rhythm is sinus tachycardia throughout, but atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response is one of the commonest precipitants of decompensation and would change management substantially, so it is worth confirming rather than assuming.

A reasonable bridge while non-invasive ventilation is set up, and better than leaving him on the cannula. It does not do the thing this patient needs most, which is positive airway pressure. Note also that oxygen is a treatment for hypoxaemia, not for dyspnoea; a non-hypoxaemic breathless heart failure patient does not benefit from high-flow oxygen and there is reason to think hyperoxia is unhelpful in cardiac patients.

prompt.text: Do you want a twelve lead on him? I can have it done in a minute.

case_actions.debrief_note: Mandatory, and for two reasons rather than one. The first is to look for an acute coronary occlusion driving the decompensation, which would redirect the entire case toward the catheter laboratory. The second is to identify a tachyarrhythmia, since new atrial fibrillation is among the most common precipitants of acute decompensation in a patient with a fixed low ejection fraction. Here the ECG is neither: sinus tachycardia with left ventricular hypertrophy and the old anterior infarct pattern. Recognising an unchanged old infarct pattern as old is itself a skill worth practising.

prompt.text: Do you want a portable chest film? Radiography is free at the moment.

case_actions.debrief_note: Supports the diagnosis and, more usefully, excludes the alternatives that would change management: pneumothorax, lobar consolidation, a large effusion. Be careful how much weight learners put on it. A meaningful minority of patients with acute decompensated heart failure have a chest film that is not obviously congested, particularly early and particularly in chronically remodelled lungs, so a normal-looking film does not exclude the diagnosis. Note the result freezing behaviour in this engine: a film ordered before intubation shows no endotracheal tube even if it arrives afterwards.
references: Wang CS, FitzGerald JM, Schulzer M, Mak E, Ayas NT. Does this dyspneic patient in the emergency department have congestive heart failure? JAMA. 2005;294(15):1944-56. [UNVERIFIED, confirm before release]

case_actions.turnaround_override_rationale: Section 8.1 of the system design permits per-study overrides but expects them unused. Bedside ultrasound is performed by the treating clinician and returns in real time; the imaging class of 10 seconds would misrepresent it. Flagged as a request for a 'bedside' turnaround class in the catalog rather than a per-case override.
case_actions.debrief_note: The fastest way to separate cardiogenic from non-cardiogenic dyspnoea at the bedside. Diffuse bilateral B-lines with a plethoric inferior vena cava and a visibly poor left ventricle is close to diagnostic in this context, and the whole study takes under two minutes. It also answers the question the physical examination cannot: whether this patient is warm and wet or cold and wet, which determines whether he gets vasodilated or supported.
references: Lichtenstein DA, Meziere GA. Relevance of lung ultrasound in the diagnosis of acute respiratory failure: the BLUE protocol. Chest. 2008;134(1):117-25. [UNVERIFIED, confirm before release]

prompt.text: Did you want to ask him about his tablets? He said something to the medics about running out.

case_actions.debrief_note: Finding the precipitant is part of the resuscitation, not paperwork for the admitting team. Decompensation in a patient with stable chronic heart failure almost always has a reason: missed diuretic, dietary sodium, new atrial fibrillation, ischaemia, infection, anaemia, thyroid disease, or a newly started negative inotrope or NSAID. Here it is a loop diuretic he stopped taking five days ago plus a salt load. That answer changes the admission plan, changes the discharge plan, and is the modifiable part of this presentation. A resident who stabilises the physiology but never asks why it happened has treated the episode and not the patient.

prerequisites.failure_message: He isn't sedated. We need an induction agent before we tube him.
He hasn't had a paralytic. We need that before we tube him.

case_actions.debrief_note: Not a harmful action, and not a scored error, but in this case it was avoidable and it cost the patient. Most patients with acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema who receive early positive pressure do not need a tube. This patient was hypercapnic and tiring, which frightens people into intubating, but hypercapnia in acute pulmonary edema is usually a fatigue phenomenon that corrects with non-invasive support rather than an independent indication for a tube. When intubation is genuinely required, anticipate the collapse rather than react to it: this patient is preload-dependent, vasodilated on a nitrate infusion, and about to receive both an induction agent that removes his sympathetic drive and positive intrathoracic pressure that reduces venous return. Have a vasopressor drawn up before you push the drugs. Post-intubation hypotension is common in emergency airway management and predicts poor outcome.
references: Heffner AC, Swords DS, Nussbaum ML, Kline JA, Jones AE. Predictors of the complication of postintubation hypotension during emergency airway management. J Crit Care. 2012;27(6):587-93. [UNVERIFIED, confirm before release]
Gray A, et al. N Engl J Med. 2008;359(2):142-51. [PubMed record checked]

case_actions.debrief_note: A defensible induction agent here. Its indirect sympathomimetic effect is often protective in shock states, though that depends on endogenous catecholamine reserve that a patient in extremis may have already exhausted, and it is a direct myocardial depressant when that reserve is gone. In this patient, who is hypertensive and tachycardic before induction, the reserve is intact.

Note that he does have chronic kidney disease; renal impairment alone is not a contraindication to succinylcholine, but a pre-existing hyperkalaemia would be, and in this case the potassium is known before intubation only if someone sent a chemistry panel.

case_actions.debrief_note: A paralysed, unsedated patient is awake and unable to move or signal. This is the canonical follow-up requirement rather than a prerequisite, precisely because it cannot be satisfied before the intubation it follows. Choose the agent with the blood pressure in mind: a propofol infusion in a patient who is already hypotensive will make it worse, and an analgesia-first approach with fentanyl, or ketamine, is usually kinder to the haemodynamics.

case_actions.debrief_note: Six to eight millilitres per kilogram of predicted body weight, calculated from height rather than actual weight. In this patient, positive end-expiratory pressure is doing useful work against the pulmonary edema, so it should not be abandoned wholesale when the pressure falls; it is one contributor among several and reducing it is a lever, not the first move.

case_actions.debrief_note: A legitimate lever in post-intubation hypotension, since high intrathoracic pressure reduces venous return. It is a trade in this patient: the same positive pressure is treating his pulmonary edema. Reduce it thoughtfully and watch the saturation, rather than dropping it to zero reflexively.

prerequisite_overrides.author_rationale: The catalog default requiring central venous access before a vasopressor is waived in this case. Short-duration peripheral administration through a well-sited proximal cannula with close monitoring is accepted practice and delaying pressure support in post-intubation collapse to place a central line is the greater harm. Extravasation risk from short peripheral vasopressor courses is low in the published series, though those series are observational.

prompt.text: Pressure is 74 over 46 since the tube went in. Do you want me to start a pressor? I can run norepinephrine through the big cannula in his elbow.

case_actions.halt_reason: You started a vasopressor in a patient with a systolic pressure of 188 who was already well perfused; the additional afterload on a failing left ventricle worsened his pulmonary edema and he arrested.
case_actions.debrief_note: The correct haemodynamic support for this patient once he is hypotensive after intubation. He has become cold and wet: the problem is now perfusion pressure, not congestion. Norepinephrine is generally preferred over epinephrine in cardiogenic shock, where a randomised comparison was stopped early for a higher rate of refractory shock in the epinephrine arm. Giving a vasopressor to the same patient while he is hypertensive is a different action entirely, which is why the tag on this entry is phase-dependent.
references: Levy B, Clere-Jehl R, Legras A, et al. Epinephrine versus norepinephrine for cardiogenic shock after acute myocardial infarction. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2018;72(2):173-82. [UNVERIFIED, confirm before release]

case_actions.halt_reason: You gave push-dose epinephrine to a patient with a systolic pressure of 188 who was already well perfused; the abrupt rise in afterload and myocardial oxygen demand on a failing ischaemic ventricle precipitated arrest.
case_actions.debrief_note: An acceptable temporising measure while an infusion is prepared, and better than watching a pressure of 74 while the pump is being spiked. It is a bridge, not a plan; boluses of a short-acting catecholamine produce peaks and troughs, and this patient needs a titratable infusion. Dosing errors with push-dose pressors are well described and the preparation step is where they happen.

prerequisites.failure_message: No line in yet.

case_actions.halt_reason: You gave intravenous metoprolol to a patient in acute decompensated heart failure whose cardiac output depended on his heart rate and endogenous adrenergic drive; acute beta blockade dropped stroke volume and rate together, and he progressed to cardiogenic shock and arrested.
case_actions.debrief_note: This is the classic trap in this case and the reason the sinus tachycardia is set at 118. The tachycardia is compensatory: it is how a ventricle with an ejection fraction of 25 percent maintains cardiac output. Removing it removes the compensation. Chronic beta blockade improves survival in HFrEF and that is exactly why residents reach for it, but initiating or up-titrating beta blockade during acute decompensation is a different intervention with different physiology, and guidelines advise against it until the patient is compensated. Note the separate question of whether to continue his home carvedilol: in a patient without hypoperfusion, continuing the home dose is usually reasonable, but that is a decision about maintaining a chronic drug, not about pushing five milligrams into a decompensated ventricle.
references: Heidenreich PA, et al. 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure. Circulation. 2022;145(18):e895-e1032. [UNVERIFIED, confirm before release]

prerequisites.failure_message: No line in yet.

case_actions.halt_reason: You gave intravenous diltiazem, a negative inotrope, to a patient with an ejection fraction of 25 percent in acute decompensation; contractility fell further, cardiac output collapsed, and he arrested.
case_actions.debrief_note: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are negatively inotropic and are contraindicated in decompensated HFrEF. The trap is dressed as rate control for the tachycardia, exactly as intravenous metoprolol is. Two separate errors are bundled here: treating a compensatory sinus tachycardia as though it were an arrhythmia, and choosing an agent that suppresses contractility in a patient with almost none to spare. If this patient were in atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response, diltiazem would still be the wrong drug for the same reason.

case_actions.halt_reason: You gave a litre of crystalloid to a patient already several litres fluid overloaded with cardiogenic pulmonary edema; the added preload raised his pulmonary venous pressure further, his oxygenation failed, and he arrested.
case_actions.debrief_note: The commonest reflex to a tachycardic, unwell-looking patient, and the wrong one here. Every finding in front of you points away from hypovolaemia: raised jugular venous pressure, an S3, bilateral crackles, peripheral edema, four kilograms above his dry weight, and a systolic pressure of 188. This is worth dwelling on in the debrief because the same reflex is correct in the septic patient two beds over, and the discriminating skill is the volume assessment rather than the general rule. Note that this remains harmful in the post-intubation hypotension phase: the hypotension there is vasodilation and reduced venous return in a fluid-overloaded patient, and the treatment is a vasopressor and stopping the nitrate, not volume.
case_actions.binding_note: Bound to normal_saline_1l_bolus and covers the other three crystalloid boluses. The resident sees four separate agents with catalog names; all four carry this action's harmful tag.

case_actions.halt_reason: You started dobutamine in a hypertensive, warm, well-perfused patient with an ischaemic cardiomyopathy; the rise in myocardial oxygen demand and its arrhythmogenic effect precipitated sustained ventricular tachycardia with haemodynamic collapse.
case_actions.debrief_note: Inotropes belong to the cold profile, not the warm one. This patient is congested but perfusing: warm extremities, normal capillary refill, a normal lactate, adequate mental status, and a systolic pressure of 188. There is nothing for an inotrope to fix and a great deal for it to destabilise in a heart with an old anterior infarct. Inotrope exposure in acute decompensated heart failure has been associated with more arrhythmia and hypotension without outcome benefit, and the routine-use trial in patients not requiring inotropic support was negative. This is the most debatable harmful designation in the case: the physiological argument is strong, but calling a single dobutamine order immediately lethal is a modelling choice made for teaching emphasis, and the reviewing physician should decide whether it should instead be a deterioration path.
references: Cuffe MS, Califf RM, Adams KF Jr, et al. Short-term intravenous milrinone for acute exacerbation of chronic heart failure: a randomized controlled trial (OPTIME-CHF). JAMA. 2002;287(12):1541-7. [UNVERIFIED, confirm before release]

case_actions.debrief_note: Morphine was taught for decades as a treatment for acute pulmonary edema on the reasoning that it reduces preload and relieves the distressing sensation of breathlessness. That rationale has not held up. Observational data, most prominently a large registry analysis, found morphine use independently associated with higher mortality, more mechanical ventilation, more intensive care admission and longer stay; a later propensity-matched registry analysis pointed the same way. The evidence is observational and confounding by indication is a serious limitation, since the sickest and most distressed patients are the ones who get morphine. So the honest summary is not that morphine kills, but that the benefit was never demonstrated, the harm signal is consistent across datasets, and there is a better tool for the same problem: the distress in this patient is caused by hypoxaemia and work of breathing, and non-invasive ventilation treats the cause rather than blunting the perception of it. This action is tagged neutral only because the tag vocabulary has no intermediate value between neutral and case-halting harm.
references: Peacock WF, Hollander JE, Diercks DB, Lopatin M, Fonarow G, Emerman CL. Morphine and outcomes in acute decompensated heart failure: an ADHERE analysis. Emerg Med J. 2008;25(4):205-9. [PubMed record checked]

Miro O, Gil V, Martin-Sanchez FJ, et al. Morphine use in the emergency department and outcomes of patients with acute heart failure: a propensity score-matching analysis based on the EAHFE Registry. Chest. 2017;152(4):821-32. [citation seen in secondary sources; verify]

case_actions.debrief_note: This is the cardiac asthma trap and the wheeze on his chest is deliberately there to bait it. Peribronchial edema narrows small airways and produces expiratory wheeze that sounds exactly like bronchospasm. The distinguishing features are all present: raised jugular venous pressure, an S3, bilateral crackles under the wheeze, peripheral edema, orthopnoea, and no history of obstructive lung disease. A beta agonist does not treat pulmonary edema. It does increase heart rate and myocardial oxygen demand in a patient with an ischaemic cardiomyopathy, and it drives potassium intracellularly in a patient about to receive a loop diuretic. When you genuinely cannot tell, treating both is defensible; assuming bronchospasm without examining the neck veins is not.

case_actions.debrief_note: Reasonable to consider and unsupported once you look. He is afebrile at 36.8, his white count is normal at 8.2, his chest film shows a symmetrical interstitial pattern with effusions rather than consolidation, and the history is days of orthopnoea and weight gain rather than cough and fever. Infection is a common precipitant of decompensation and worth actively excluding, so the thought is right; committing to it here means ignoring the answer the workup already gave you. The mildly raised lactate of 2.1 is a work-of-breathing phenomenon, not evidence of sepsis, and it is the finding most likely to pull a learner down this path.

Low cost and low harm, and he takes 81 mg daily at home anyway. The reason it appears in the debrief is what it usually signals: a learner who saw a troponin of 62 and started an acute coronary syndrome pathway. The troponin here is a type 2 injury pattern, demand ischaemia from tachycardia and wall stress in a hypertrophied, chronically infarcted ventricle, and it is accompanied by an ECG with no acute ischaemic change. Almost all patients with acute decompensated heart failure have a detectable troponin on a high-sensitivity assay, and a modestly raised value is prognostic rather than diagnostic. The question to ask is not whether the troponin is elevated but whether the pattern, the ECG and the story fit acute coronary occlusion. Here they do not.

Ordered without a pretest probability, and it comes back at 0.94, which is what a D-dimer does in a 65 year old with heart failure. It was never going to be negative and it cannot exclude anything in a patient in whom you have not first established that pulmonary embolism is a plausible diagnosis. Consider what the history already gave you: five days of progressive orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, weight gain and leg swelling that is symmetrical, no calf asymmetry, no immobility, no malignancy, no recent surgery. The teaching point is test discipline. An unindicated test with a foreseeable abnormal result generates a CT angiogram, a contrast load, and an anchoring error.

Not indicated, and getting there usually means an unindicated D-dimer came back positive. The concrete costs are the radiation, the cost, and above all removing a patient in respiratory distress on non-invasive ventilation from a resuscitation area to lie flat in a scanner, which is the real hazard here rather than the contrast. On contrast and the kidneys, be careful what you teach: contrast-associated acute kidney injury is a genuine entity, but the risk attributable to contrast has been substantially overstated in older literature that lacked control groups, and more recent propensity-matched work suggests a far smaller effect than was once believed. Withholding a genuinely indicated scan out of renal fear is its own error. The reason not to scan this patient is that he does not need it.

A titratable vasodilator in a patient whose pressure you intend to move substantially requires blood pressure measurement at an interval short enough to catch an overshoot. Cycling every fifteen minutes while running nitroglycerin is how a patient ends up hypotensive between readings.

Diuretic response is the measurement that tells you whether your treatment worked, and it is the earliest signal of diuretic resistance. Documented output also matters for the admitting team, who will titrate against it. Note that this does not require a urinary catheter; a bottle and a nurse who records the volume is enough, and avoids the catheter-associated infection risk in an admitted patient.

Defensible in a patient who is about to be heavily diuresed, on non-invasive ventilation, and unable to get to a toilet, and it becomes clearly appropriate if he is intubated. It is not a mandatory part of managing acute heart failure, and reflexive catheterisation of every diuresed patient carries an infection cost. A reasoned choice either way.

Screens for anaemia, which is both a precipitant of decompensation and a marker of worse outcomes in heart failure, and for the leukocytosis that would support an infective trigger. Here the haemoglobin of 12.4 is mildly low and worth noting on the admission problem list, and the normal white count argues against infection.

Essential before and during diuresis. Three things matter here. The sodium of 133 is dilutional and is an established marker of worse prognosis in heart failure, not simply a number to correct. The creatinine of 1.62 against a baseline of 1.4 is cardiorenal physiology, driven substantially by venous congestion rather than by poor forward flow, and it is not a reason to withhold diuresis; decongestion often improves it. The potassium will fall as you diurese, in a patient on digoxin-free but arrhythmia-prone ground, so it needs rechecking.

Most useful when the diagnosis is uncertain, which in this presentation it is not. A value of 9600 pg/mL is strongly supportive but it is not the reason to treat, and treating the number rather than the patient is the failure mode. Know what shifts it: it rises with age, renal impairment and atrial fibrillation, and it is lowered by obesity, so a value that looks unimpressive in a heavy patient may still be meaningful. In a patient with chronic heart failure, the comparison that matters is against his own previous values rather than against a population threshold.
references: Maisel AS, Krishnaswamy P, Nowak RM, et al. Rapid measurement of B-type natriuretic peptide in the emergency diagnosis of heart failure. N Engl J Med. 2002;347(3):161-7. [UNVERIFIED, confirm before release]

case_actions.debrief_note: Appropriate to send, and the interpretation is the teaching point rather than the ordering. See the note on aspirin: a mildly raised troponin in acute decompensated heart failure is usual, reflects demand ischaemia and wall stress, and carries prognostic weight without implying acute coronary occlusion. A single value cannot distinguish acute from chronic elevation; a delta on a repeat sample is what does that, and in this engine a repeat requires an explicit second order.

The most useful single test in the first two minutes. His pH of 7.29 with a pCO2 of 54 shows an acute respiratory acidosis: he is tiring, not simply hypoxaemic. That finding frightens people toward intubation, but hypercapnia in acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema is usually fatigue and it corrects with positive pressure. The gas after non-invasive ventilation, if repeated, demonstrates exactly that.

A useful perfusion check that supports the warm rather than cold classification. The value of 2.1 is mildly raised and is explained by the work of respiratory muscles, not by circulatory failure. Reading it as evidence of sepsis or of cardiogenic shock in a patient with warm peripheries, normal mentation and a systolic pressure of 188 is a common misstep.

Not required, and mildly informative if sent. The transaminase and bilirubin pattern here is congestive hepatopathy from raised right-sided filling pressures, matching the tender enlarged liver on examination. It is a congestion finding rather than a hepatic problem in its own right.

Reasonable to send alongside potassium in a patient about to receive loop diuretics, since magnesium losses accompany potassium losses and unreplaced hypomagnesemia makes hypokalaemia refractory. Normal here.

Part of a precipitant search rather than an emergency test. Thyrotoxicosis and profound hypothyroidism can both decompensate a failing ventricle, and it is a sensible inpatient investigation. It will not change anything in the next hour.
Neutral. Part of an infection screen if you are pursuing one; not informative here.

Appropriate to request for the admission, not available on the timescale of this resuscitation, and not needed to make the decisions in front of you. Bedside ultrasound answers the immediate questions about ventricular function, filling and B-lines; the formal study answers the questions about valve lesions and quantified ejection fraction that will guide his inpatient therapy.

Appropriate, and more useful once you have an ECG and a troponin to discuss, since the first question you will be asked is whether this is ischaemic. Calling before the workup exists produces a conversation about what to order rather than about what to do.

A patient on non-invasive ventilation with a titrating vasoactive infusion needs a bed that can continue both. Making that call early shortens the time to an appropriate bed, which is often the rate-limiting step in the department.

Premature. A creatinine of 1.62 against a baseline of 1.4 in a congested patient is cardiorenal physiology, and the treatment for it is decongestion rather than renal replacement. Urgent dialysis is indicated for refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, uraemic complications, or diuretic-refractory fluid overload, none of which is present. The call is not harmful; it is a signal that the creatinine was read as a kidney problem rather than as a heart problem seen through the kidney.
Completion of the case. Scored on disposition and diagnosis separately; see the handoff section.

Reasonable but rarely necessary here, and it should not delay treatment. It gives beat-to-beat pressure while titrating a vasodilator, which is genuinely useful, and it becomes more attractive if the patient is intubated and on a vasopressor. Frequent non-invasive cycling achieves most of the benefit in a patient who is improving. Placing one before applying positive pressure would be a clear misordering of priorities.

In a breathless patient the airway question is answered by listening to him talk. Speech fragmented into two or three word bursts is a measurement of respiratory reserve, not a communication problem, and it is the finding that tells you how close he is to tiring. A patient who can still protect his airway and speak does not need a tube yet, however bad he looks.

Work of breathing is the end-of-bed assessment and it does most of the triage in this case. Upright posture the patient will not abandon, accessory muscle use, intercostal indrawing and diaphoresis together identify a patient who needs an intervention in the next few minutes rather than the next hour. This is also the finding that improves first and most visibly with non-invasive ventilation, which makes it the one to re-check after you act.

This is the manoeuvre that decides the case. Warm peripheries with a capillary refill under two seconds and full pulses place him in the warm profile, which is what makes vasodilation and diuresis safe and inotropes wrong. The same patient after intubation is cool and mottled with a four second refill, and the treatment inverts. Perfusion is not a number on the monitor; it is this examination.

The single most useful physical sign in this case, and the one most often skipped. A raised jugular venous pressure separates this patient from the septic patient who needs fluid and from the asthmatic who needs bronchodilators. Auscultating the chest without also looking at the neck veins is how the wheeze gets misread as bronchospasm. The hepatojugular reflux is the confirmatory manoeuvre when the column is technically difficult to see, which it often is in a heavy, breathless patient who will not lie back; a sustained rise that does not fall back while pressure is maintained is a positive test.

A third heart sound is one of the few examination findings in dyspnoea with a high positive likelihood ratio for heart failure. It is insensitive, so its absence proves little, but hearing it in this context is close to diagnostic. The laterally displaced apex is chronic, not acute. The symmetrical pitting edema measures how long this has been building; it is days of accumulated sodium and water, and it will not resolve in the emergency department however much you diurese.

Crackles with an overlying expiratory wheeze. Cardiac asthma is the trap: the wheeze is deliberate and it is there to attract a bronchodilator. What settles it is not the chest at all, it is the neck veins and the peripheries.

The tender enlarged liver is congestive hepatopathy from raised right-sided pressures, and it matches the abnormal liver enzymes if those were sent. It also matters as a negative: a soft abdomen without peritonism moves an intra-abdominal catastrophe well down the list in a patient who is tachycardic and unwell.

Here this is a pertinent negative and nothing else. Symmetrical edema with no calf tenderness, asymmetry or cords argues against deep vein thrombosis, which is the reasoning that should stop the D-dimer being sent rather than the D-dimer result stopping it afterwards.

Peripheral temperature and sweating are the two bedside proxies for perfusion and sympathetic drive. He is sweating heavily but his skin is warm, which is the sympathetic response to respiratory distress rather than the vasoconstriction of shock. Cold and sweaty would mean something entirely different and would change the treatment.

Mental status is a perfusion measurement, and here it is the reassuring one. A patient who is alert, oriented and anxious is perfusing his brain, which supports the warm classification and argues against cardiogenic shock. A patient with the same vital signs who has become drowsy is a different and much more urgent problem.

Anxiety in acute pulmonary edema is a symptom of hypoxaemia and air hunger, not a psychiatric finding, and it settles as the physiology settles. Recording it matters because it is the baseline against which a later change in mental state is judged.

follow_ups.nurse_prompt: He's tubed and he's still paralysed from the rocuronium. Do you want to write him up for something for sedation and pain?
follow_ups.debrief_note: A paralysed patient without sedation is awake, aware, and unable to signal. This obligation is created by the intubation and cannot precede it, which is why it is modelled as a follow-up rather than a prerequisite. Choose an agent with the blood pressure in mind.

follow_ups.nurse_prompt: Do you want a film to check the tube position? Any film you ordered before the tube went in won't show it.
follow_ups.debrief_note: Radiographic confirmation of tube depth is standard after intubation and does not replace waveform capnography, which confirms tracheal placement. The engine detail matters here: results freeze at the state in which they were ordered, so a chest film requested before intubation will not show the tube even if it arrives afterwards. A repeat order is required.

follow_ups.nurse_prompt: The nitro is running. The cuff is set to cycle every fifteen minutes at the moment. Do you want it more often than that?
follow_ups.debrief_note: A titratable vasodilator needs a measurement interval short enough to catch an overshoot before it becomes symptomatic. Fifteen-minute cycling while titrating nitroglycerin is how a patient becomes hypotensive between readings.

follow_ups.nurse_prompt: He's had his diuretic. Do you want me to start recording his urine output?
follow_ups.debrief_note: Diuretic response is how you find out whether your treatment is working and is the earliest indicator of diuretic resistance. It does not require a urinary catheter.

follow_up_condition_note: None of the four applies_when conditions above does discriminating work in this case; each is trivially true once its trigger has fired. That is honest rather than clever: the mechanism exists for cases where an obligation applies only sometimes. Flagged so the reviewer does not mistake the conditions for meaningful clinical gating.

consult_cardiology.value: Cardiology fellow: I have looked at the tracing. This sounds like straightforward volume and afterload decompensation, most likely because he stopped his diuretic. consult_nephrology.value: Nephrology fellow: I have seen the chemistry. A creatinine of 1.6 against a baseline of 1.4 in a congested patient is not an indication for anything from us. That is cardiorenal, and it is mostly venous congestion transmitted back to the kidney rather than poor forward flow. The treatment is to decongest him, and his creatinine may well rise a little while you do that, which is expected and is not a reason to stop. There is no hyperkalaemia, no severe acidosis, no uraemic complication. Call us back if he genuinely does not respond to diuresis.

authoring_notes.alertness_gating: Section 10.5 asks for alertness gating authored once as a global rule. The condition language has no alertness predicate, so alertness must be reached indirectly through the phases that carry it. The global rule below enumerates the two phases in this case where alertness level is 3. Flagged in the review packet as a language gap.
authoring_notes.breathlessness_gating: Section 10.5 covers alertness but not speech limited by respiratory distress. This patient is fully alert in the presentation phase and can answer, but only in short bursts. That could not be done as a global rule without suppressing all topic content, so every topic carries its own presentation-phase answer. Ellipses mark where he stops to breathe.
authoring_notes.interview_during_niv: In the stabilizing phase the patient has a mask on his face. The answers assume the mask is lifted briefly, which is what actually happens at the bedside. This is deliberately not modelled as a barrier, because penalising a resident for correctly applying non-invasive ventilation before taking a history would teach the wrong lesson. The debrief note on history timing carries the real teaching point instead.
authoring_notes.diagnosis_disclosure: Section 10.4 forbids the patient from stating or implying the diagnosis. He does describe his known chronic history in lay terms, including that his heart was damaged by a previous infarct, because that is required past medical history content and a real patient would volunteer it. He never attributes the current episode to a cause and never uses the words heart failure. This line is a judgement call and is flagged for the reviewing physician.
authoring_notes.coverage_exceptions: Pregnancy status is not authored; the patient is a 65 year old man and section 10.2 requires it only where applicable. Code status and goals of care are not authored, though they are a defensible conversation in an admission for decompensated heart failure; noted as a possible addition.

correct_disposition.label: Intensive care unit or coronary care unit
correct_disposition.explanation: He is on non-invasive ventilation with a titrating vasoactive infusion. That combination requires a unit that can continue both and reassess frequently, which in most institutions means intensive care or a coronary care unit. If he was intubated during the case, the answer is unambiguously intensive care.

alternative_dispositions.label: Step-down or high dependency unit with telemetry
alternative_dispositions.explanation: Defensible, and at many institutions this is where this patient actually goes. Whether it is correct depends entirely on local capability: a step-down unit that can maintain non-invasive ventilation and titrate a nitrate infusion with frequent blood pressure measurement is an appropriate destination, and one that cannot is not. The reasoning matters more than the label, and a learner who chose this and can articulate what the unit needs to be able to do has understood the question. If the patient was intubated, this becomes wrong.

alternative_dispositions.label: General medical ward with telemetry
alternative_dispositions.explanation: A general ward cannot run non-invasive ventilation or a titrating vasodilator, and the nursing ratio does not support the frequency of reassessment this patient needs in the next few hours. The judgement error is treating clinical improvement as though it were resolution. He looks much better than he did on arrival, which is exactly what makes this the tempting wrong answer: he is better because of two interventions that a general ward cannot continue.

alternative_dispositions.label: Emergency department observation unit
alternative_dispositions.explanation: Observation pathways for heart failure exist and are appropriate for a specific, narrow group: mild congestion, no hypoxaemia, no ventilatory support, prompt symptom response to a single diuretic dose, normal or near-baseline renal function, no troponin elevation, and no high-risk features. This patient fails almost every one of those criteria. He required positive pressure ventilation and a vasoactive infusion, his creatinine has moved from baseline, and his troponin is elevated.

alternative_dispositions.label: Discharge home with adjusted diuretic and cardiology follow-up
alternative_dispositions.explanation: Unsafe. He presented in respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support, and the fact that he improved rapidly does not undo that. The precipitant is fixable and the temptation is to think that restarting the diuretic solves it, but he is still several kilograms above his dry weight, still congested, has a rise in creatinine, and has a raised troponin. Early mortality after an admission for decompensated heart failure is substantial, and this is not a presentation that gets sent home from the department.

alternative_dispositions.label: Direct to the cardiac catheterisation laboratory
alternative_dispositions.explanation: Selecting this almost always means the raised troponin was read as an acute coronary occlusion. The ECG shows an established anterior infarct pattern with no acute ST elevation, no new depression and no reciprocal change, and the troponin elevation is a demand pattern in a decompensated ventricle. Acute coronary syndrome remains a common precipitant of decompensation and deserves inpatient consideration, but nothing here justifies emergent revascularisation.

correct_diagnosis.label: Acute decompensated heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, with cardiogenic pulmonary edema
correct_diagnosis.explanation: Acute on chronic decompensation of known HFrEF, presenting as hypertensive acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema, precipitated by loop diuretic non-adherence and a dietary sodium load. Warm and wet, Nohria profile B.
correct_diagnosis.label_note: Label retained for the review packet. The interface shows the diagnosis catalog's own display name, which is shorter.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: The wheeze invites this and the smoking history supports it, which is why it is the commonest wrong answer to this presentation. What argues against it: no diagnosis of obstructive lung disease, no chronic productive cough, orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, a raised jugular venous pressure, an S3, symmetrical peripheral edema, nine pounds of weight gain, and a chest film showing interstitial edema with effusions rather than hyperinflation. Wheeze in this patient is peribronchial edema, not bronchospasm. The two conditions coexist often enough that this needs active exclusion rather than assumption.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Community-acquired pneumonia
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Reasonable to consider in an older patient with dyspnoea and crackles, and excluded by the data available. He is afebrile, his white count is normal, there are no sick contacts and no preceding coryzal illness, and the radiograph shows a symmetrical interstitial pattern with effusions rather than focal consolidation. The lactate of 2.1 is the finding most likely to mislead, and it is explained by respiratory muscle work. Infection is a frequent precipitant of decompensation, so the correct posture is to look for it and then let the evidence settle it.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Acute pulmonary embolism
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Usually selected downstream of an unindicated D-dimer. The pretest probability is low: symptoms progressed over days rather than abruptly, there is no pleuritic pain, no haemoptysis, no immobility or travel or surgery, and the leg swelling is symmetrical without calf tenderness. Positive findings point elsewhere, particularly orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, a raised venous pressure and an S3. Submassive pulmonary embolism can certainly present as breathlessness in a cardiac patient, but it does not usually come with nine pounds of weight gain and a story of a missed diuretic.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: The troponin is elevated, so this is not an unreasonable thought, but it confuses myocardial injury with myocardial infarction. Type 2 injury from demand ischaemia is expected in a decompensated ventricle with tachycardia, hypertension and hypertrophy, and almost all such patients have a detectable high-sensitivity troponin. Acute coronary syndrome requires an ischaemic story or ischaemic ECG change alongside a rising and falling pattern. He denies chest pain, is explicit that this feels nothing like his previous infarct, and his ECG shows an unchanged old anterior infarct. It stays on the inpatient differential; it is not the leading diagnosis.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Asthma exacerbation
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Follows the same error as the obstructive lung disease answer and is less defensible in a 65 year old with no history of asthma. New wheeze at this age in a patient with known cardiomyopathy is cardiac until proven otherwise.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Acute respiratory distress syndrome
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Bilateral infiltrates with hypoxaemia meet part of the definition, but ARDS requires that the respiratory failure is not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload, and here it is entirely explained by exactly that. There is also no ARDS precipitant: no sepsis, aspiration, pancreatitis, trauma or transfusion. The raised jugular venous pressure, S3, plethoric inferior vena cava and severely impaired left ventricle all point to a cardiogenic mechanism.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Sepsis of unclear source
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Selecting this usually means the lactate of 2.1 was read as evidence of shock. He is afebrile with a normal white count, warm and hypertensive with brisk capillary refill and clear mentation, and has no identified source. Hyperlactataemia from work of breathing is a genuine and common phenomenon. The clinical cost of this answer is not academic: it is the fluid bolus that follows it.

additional_diagnoses.label: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema
additional_diagnoses.explanation: The presentation itself: bilateral B lines, bilateral crackles, a saturation of 87 percent and a respiratory rate of 32 in a man whose ventricle cannot cope with the afterload of a systolic pressure of 188. Named beside the heart failure it says what the heart failure did; named alone it leaves out why.

additional_diagnoses.label: Acute hypercapnic respiratory failure
additional_diagnoses.explanation: A venous pH of 7.29 with a pCO2 of 54 in a patient breathing at 32 is a man who is moving air and not clearing carbon dioxide with it, which is the reason bilevel positive pressure rather than oxygen alone is the treatment, and the reason the receiving team needs to know how close he came to a tube.

additional_diagnoses.label: Hypertensive emergency
additional_diagnoses.explanation: A systolic pressure of 188 with acute pulmonary edema is hypertensive emergency by definition: end-organ dysfunction attributable to the pressure. It is the reason nitrates are the pharmacological priority here, and a handover that names it explains the nitroglycerin infusion to whoever inherits it.

additional_diagnoses.label: Hyponatraemia
additional_diagnoses.explanation: A sodium of 133 is mild and dilutional, and it is worth naming at handover for what it is rather than what to do about it: an established marker of worse prognosis in heart failure, and a reason to watch the free water rather than to correct the number.

clinical_domains.label: History taking and identifying the precipitant

debrief_configuration.key_exams_note: v0.9. Read by the summary's Physical score when no exam carries a critical or recommended tag, as none does in this case. Regions where this case's findings are made or excluded. Author judgement by an AI assistant, unreviewed.
cross_cutting_teaching_points: The organising framework for this case is the warm-and-wet profile. Congestion determines whether the patient needs decongestion and vasodilation; perfusion determines whether they can tolerate it. This patient is congested and perfusing, so vasodilate and decongest, and do not support with inotropes or fluid. The same patient after intubation becomes cold and wet, and the treatment changes accordingly. Teaching the axes rather than the recipe is what transfers to the next case.

Sequencing is the skill this case tests, not recall. Nearly every learner knows that heart failure is treated with a diuretic. Fewer recognise that in the first ten minutes of hypertensive acute pulmonary edema, positive pressure and afterload reduction do more than the diuretic does, and that the diuretic is treating the days of accumulated sodium and water rather than the crisis in front of you.

Two of the four halting actions in this case, intravenous metoprolol and diltiazem, are attempts to treat a compensatory sinus tachycardia. Recognising a tachycardia as compensation rather than pathology is a discrete, transferable skill.

The precipitant is part of the diagnosis. Acute decompensated heart failure is not a complete formulation; acute decompensated heart failure because he ran out of furosemide and ate a salt load is, and only the second version generates a plan that prevents the readmission.
debrief_configuration.attempt_history_note: This case rewards replay. A learner who halts the case on intravenous metoprolol and then runs it cleanly has learned the thing the case exists to teach.
debrief_configuration.trap_actions_note: Plausible-looking actions that are wrong here. They are currently tagged neutral and so carry no scoring weight; retagging them 'discouraged' is outstanding. See authored_against.conformance_note.

phases_note: label is the full clinical description used in the debrief; short_label is what fits on the monitor beside the vitals. Keep short_label to a few words. v0.7: oxygen_saturation is authored as the UNSUPPORTED baseline in every non-terminal phase, and is 87 in presentation, stabilizing and improving. What the monitor reads is that baseline plus whatever vital_effects are acting, so the only things that raise this patient's saturation are positive pressure and, briefly, a nitrate. Diuresis moves heart rate, blood pressure and respiratory rate and moves the saturation by nothing, which is the case's second learning objective made mechanical rather than asserted. The terminal phases are exempt from effects and read exactly as authored. case_complete is one authored snapshot regardless of the path taken to it, as it always was. It now reads 90, the number a patient on positive pressure has been showing for most of the run, so handing off does not jump the monitor six points on the way to the debrief.
